summary:
Live site: https://osu-spherex.vercel.app

SPHEREx photographs the whole sky again and again, which means anything that moves or changes brightness leaves a trace in its images. That is how Pluto was found in 1930, by comparing photographs taken on different nights, and the same idea is behind today's searches for a "Planet X". Our web tool lets anyone do this comparison in a browser. Type a sky position (or pick one of five examples) and the tool collects every SPHEREx image of that spot, lines them up, and plays them as a short film. A difference view shows what moved between two visits. A "shift-and-stack" view adds up dozens of images along a chosen direction of motion, so an object too faint to see in any single image appears, as the cold brown dwarf WISE 0855 does; a search mode tries every direction by itself. For each source the tool measures the motion in arcseconds per year and the brightness over time, taking care to compare only images taken at the same wavelength, because every SPHEREx image sees a source in a different colour. On the test objects the measurements agree with published catalogues: Barnard's Star moves north by 10.26 ± 0.15 arcseconds per year (catalogue: 10.36), the brown dwarf Epsilon Indi B is found to be 3.3 parsecs away from SPHEREx images alone (catalogue: 3.7), and the variable stars RW Aurigae and R Draconis change brightness by factors of 2.5 and 3.9.
details:
Try it: https://osu-spherex.vercel.app (mirror: https://osu-spherex.onrender.com). How it works, with every number and its source: https://osu-spherex.vercel.app/method

What it does. The user gives a right ascension and declination. The tool finds every SPHEREx Level 2 image that covers that position through the public IRSA archive, cuts out a square of 3, 6 or 10 arcminutes from each, and resamples all of them onto one common grid (north up, 3 arcseconds per pixel), with a constant background removed from each image. This small "cube" (about 1 MB for a 3-arcminute field) is sent to the browser once. Everything interactive happens in the browser, so there is no waiting on a server: playing the images in time order, blinking between visits, subtracting one visit from another, shifting and stacking images along a motion vector, and trying every motion on a grid.

Why a film is not enough. A SPHEREx pixel is 6.16 arcseconds. Barnard's Star, the fastest star in the sky, moves 10.3 arcseconds per year, which is 1.7 pixels. A film alone barely shows it. So the tool has four views of the same images: the film, "Compare visits" (the difference image turns that small step into a clear dark-and-bright pair), "Stack" (adds the images along a motion, by hand or by a search over all motions up to 15 arcseconds per year), and "Measure" (the motion, the light curves and the spectrum as numbers). All six SPHEREx detectors, from 0.75 to 5 micrometres, can be put side by side.

Measurements are made on the original images, not on the film. Resampling smooths pixels, so positions and brightness are measured on the raw cutouts. For position, a point-source model is fitted to the valid pixels of every image, the result is converted to sky coordinates with that image's own astrometric solution, and the images of one visit are combined with a median. SPHEREx returns to a field about every six months, from opposite sides of the Earth's orbit, so a nearby star is also displaced by its parallax; where the Gaia catalogue has a parallax for the object, that yearly swing is taken out first. A straight line through the visits then gives the motion and its uncertainty. The detectors are checked against each other: if they disagree by more than their error bars allow, the error bars are widened.

Brightness is compared only at matching wavelength. SPHEREx uses a linear variable filter: where a source falls on the detector decides the wavelength at which it is seen, so every image of a source is at a different wavelength. Comparing two images directly would mistake the star's spectrum for a change in time. The tool reads the wavelength of each image at the source position, groups the measurements in bins of 0.02 micrometres, and draws one light curve per bin. The same points plotted against wavelength give a spectrum of the source at no extra cost.

Saturated stars. Very bright stars overflow their central pixels, which the SPHEREx pipeline masks. For those the tool measures the mean brightness in a ring around the star (the wings of the image of the star), which follows the star's brightness at a fixed wavelength. The tool says which method it used.

The search does not fool itself. The motion search stacks the images along every motion on a grid and reports the best one. To know whether that is more than chance, it repeats the search with the dates of the images shuffled. Only if no shuffled order scores as high does it say "motion detected"; otherwise it says "consistent" or "nothing found". On a patch of empty sky next to WISE 0855 it finds nothing.

Results on the five required objects.

- Barnard's Star: +10.26 ± 0.15 arcsec/yr north from six detectors together (catalogue +10.36); the detector the site opens with gives +9.93 ± 0.46. East-west it is −1.26 ± 0.38 (catalogue −0.80) and poorly constrained in the four detectors where the star saturates (−1.50 ± 1.43 in the first one); the tool flags this instead of hiding it. Without the parallax correction the two unsaturated detectors gave −2.8 and −3.0; with it, −0.8 and −1.0.

- Epsilon Indi B: +3.92 ± 0.12 east, −2.46 ± 0.11 north arcsec/yr (five detectors together: +3.93 ± 0.07, −2.54 ± 0.05), against +3.97, −2.54 for its companion star Epsilon Indi A, with which it travels. Left free, the parallax comes out as 0.30 ± 0.05 arcseconds from SPHEREx alone (Gaia: 0.271), a distance of 3.3 parsecs (Gaia: 3.7). Its spectrum, from the same images, has a dip near 1.4 micrometres: about 6 mJy there against about 40 mJy at 1.27 and 1.57 micrometres.

- WISE 0855: invisible in single images; it shows up when the images are stacked along its motion. The search, told nothing about the direction, picks (−8.7, +0.2) arcsec/yr; the CatWISE2020 catalogue has (−7.97, +0.81), which is 0.9 away with a grid step of 3. Below 3.8 micrometres the light at its position is another star, 8 arcseconds away, and the tool says so.

- RW Aurigae: 2.5 times brighter in September 2026 than in September 2025 at 0.74–0.76 micrometres.

- R Draconis: a factor of 3.9 between its bright and faint states at 0.94–0.96 micrometres. It is a Mira variable with a 245.6-day period.

- Control: a star with no catalogued motion, 1.3 arcminutes from Barnard's Star, stays within 0.16 arcseconds of its position in all four visits, and its brightness changes by 3% at a typical wavelength.

Honest limits. One year of data and 6-arcsecond pixels: only fast or bright movers can be measured directly. The motion search does not model parallax, so it finds nearby fast objects; a distant planet, which swings by arcminutes a year as the Earth moves, needs a wider search that does. The parallax of Barnard's Star could not be measured (0.0 ± 0.3 arcseconds against 0.547): in one of its visits the positions are damaged along detector rows, and we did not find the cause. For a position typed by the user, the motion is fitted without the parallax correction; only the prepared examples have it, where Gaia gives a parallax. On a star that saturates the detector the motion search is not stable: for Barnard's Star it lands 1.7 arcseconds per year from the catalogue value, with a grid step of 3. When the archive's image search does not answer, as on 15 November 2026, only positions near the five examples work, from a saved list of images. The archive serves two processing versions (Data Release 1 for images up to May 2026, Quick Release 3 for later ones), whose brightness scales differ by about 3%, so the tool does not claim changes smaller than about 4%.

How it is built. Python (astropy, reproject, scipy) prepares the cubes and the measurements; a FastAPI service queries IRSA with retries and a disk cache; the interface is Next.js and React with plain canvas drawing. Cubes for the five example objects are precomputed in all six detectors, so the demonstration works even when the archive is slow or down.

Who it is for. Students, amateur astronomers and curious people. Finding a moving dot is how the outer solar system was mapped. The same data that professionals will search for distant planets are public, and this tool makes the search something a person can try on a phone.

Data and credits.

NASA data. SPHEREx Level 2 spectral images, obtained from the NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA). This is the only image data the tool uses. We search for images with IRSA's Table Access Protocol service (tables spherex.plane and spherex.artifact, selecting the images whose footprint contains the requested position) and download small cutouts with IRSA's cutout service. From each file we use the calibrated image, the wavelength solution, the variance and the flag planes. IRSA began serving Data Release 1 on 14 November 2026, during the event. Since then the images taken up to May 2026 come from Data Release 1 and the later ones from Quick Release 3: of the 2,187 images listed for our five examples, 1,590 are Data Release 1 and 597 are Quick Release 3. Before the event only Quick Release 2 and 3 were public. We compared the releases on the same exposures and report the difference (about 3% in brightness scale).

Acknowledgement requested by IRSA: "This publication makes use of data products from the Spectro-Photometer for the History of the Universe, Epoch of Reionization and Ices Explorer (SPHEREx), which is a joint project of the Jet Propulsion Laboratory and the California Institute of Technology, and is funded by the National Aeronautics and Space Administration." Mission paper: Bock et al. (2026).

How we used it. Every picture, motion and light curve in the tool comes from these images. For the five example objects the cutouts were downloaded in advance (2,847 files in total: 660 from Quick Release 2 and 3 before the event, and 2,187 on 14 November, in all six detectors) and turned into ready-made image cubes, which the site marks as "from cache". For any other position the images are fetched from IRSA when the user asks. If IRSA's search does not answer, positions near the five examples use the list of images IRSA gave us on 14 November 2026, the images themselves are still fetched from IRSA, and the page says that the list is a saved one. No data are simulated or invented.

Also from NASA: CatWISE2020 (NASA's WISE mission), through IRSA: catalogue positions and motions shown as an overlay, and the reference motion of WISE 0855. Two Micron All Sky Survey (2MASS) Point Source Catalog (NASA and NSF), through IRSA: the 1999 position of Epsilon Indi B (source 2MASS J22041052−5646577), used before the event to find it in the SPHEREx images. The object was reported by Scholz et al. 2003 (A&A 398, L29).

Other references. Gaia Data Release 3 (ESA): positions, proper motions and parallaxes of Barnard's Star, Epsilon Indi A and B, RW Aurigae, R Draconis and of the comparison star, and the catalogue marks on the images. Queried through IRSA; the parallax column was taken from the ESA Gaia Archive on 15 November 2026, when IRSA's search was down. Spitzer astrometry of WISE 0855−0714, used to choose between duplicate catalogue entries: Kirkpatrick et al. 2021 (ApJS 253, 7) and Luhman & Esplin 2016 (AJ 152, 78). General Catalogue of Variable Stars (GCVS), through VizieR: variability type and period of R Draconis.

Software (all open source). Python: astropy, astroquery, pyvo, reproject, numpy, scipy, matplotlib, requests, FastAPI, pytest. Web: Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, vitest; the fonts Unbounded, IBM Plex Sans and IBM Plex Mono (all under the SIL Open Font License). Hosting: Vercel for the site, Render for the Python service and a backup copy of the site.

Our own work. All code, text and figures in the project were made by Team OSU during the event, with the AI assistance described below. Short exploratory scripts written before the event to check that the data were usable (in the experiments/ folder) are included and labelled as such; the tool itself was written after the official start.

No third-party images, video or music are used. Every picture on the site is SPHEREx data drawn by our code; the charts and the site icon (two dots, one cold and one warm: a star at two visits) are drawn by code as well.
